ecosystem-disruptions-s1.title: Algae and dissolved oxygen along a stream below a fish farm
ecosystem-disruptions-s1.text: A fish farm releases water rich in nitrogen and phosphorus (from fish wastes and uneaten food) into a stream at distance 0. On one sunny summer day, a team measured dissolved oxygen at dawn and at 3 p.m., and the concentration of algae (as chlorophyll), at sites from 1 km upstream (−1) to 10 km downstream. Water temperature was 19-20 °C at every site. Many fish are stressed when dissolved oxygen falls below about 4 mg/L.

ecosystem-disruptions-s2.title: PCB concentrations in a lake food web
ecosystem-disruptions-s2.text: PCBs are industrial chemicals that are fat-soluble and break down very slowly. Researchers measured PCBs in the water of a large lake and in organisms from its food web. Gulls eat mainly large fish. Values are means; ppm is parts per million by mass.

items.q: Which statement best describes the data downstream of the outfall?
options: Algae and both oxygen readings fall below the outfall, reaching their lowest values at 3 km.
Algae rise to a peak at 3 km, and the gap between afternoon and dawn oxygen is widest there.
Algae rise to a peak at 3 km, and oxygen rises at dawn and at 3 p.m. by the same amount there.
Algae stay near upstream levels, while dawn oxygen falls steadily over the whole 10 km.

why.correct: Chlorophyll rises from 2.2 to 11 µg/L at 3 km; there afternoon oxygen is 13.5 mg/L and dawn oxygen 3.1 mg/L, the widest gap. Farther downstream all three return toward upstream values.
options: Afternoon oxygen and algae rise below the outfall; only dawn oxygen falls.
Correct: the algae peak matches the largest day-night swing in oxygen.
Dawn oxygen falls (to 3.1 mg/L) while afternoon oxygen rises.
Algae rise five-fold, and dawn oxygen recovers after 3 km.

items.q: At 3 km downstream, how much higher is dissolved oxygen at 3 p.m. than at dawn, in mg/L? Give your answer to one decimal place.

why.correct: 13.5 − 3.1 = 10.4 mg/L. Upstream the difference is only 9.0 − 8.4 = 0.6 mg/L.

items.q: Which explanation best accounts for the oxygen readings at 3 km?
options: Algae take up O₂ by day for photosynthesis and release it at night, so the stream is richest in O₂ just after dawn.
The fish farm releases O₂-poor water at night and O₂-rich water by day, so the readings at 3 km follow the farm's daily cycle.
Water warms during the day, and warm water holds more dissolved O₂, so readings are high in the afternoon and low at dawn.
By day the dense algae add O₂ by photosynthesis; at night algae and decomposers respire without it, so O₂ falls by dawn.

why.correct: Photosynthesis adds O₂ only in light; respiration by algae, bacteria and animals uses it all the time. Where algae are dense, the daytime gain and the nighttime loss are both large.
options: Photosynthesis releases O₂; the readings are highest in the afternoon, not at dawn.
The swing is largest at 3 km, not at the outfall, and it tracks the algae, not the farm.
Temperature was 19-20 °C at every site, and warm water actually holds less O₂, not more.
Correct: photosynthesis by day, respiration around the clock.

items.q: What is the purpose of the site 1 km upstream of the outfall?
options: It shows the stream's conditions without the farm's water, as a baseline for comparison.
It is where the nutrients released by the farm are most concentrated in the stream.
It measures how far upstream the algae from the bloom can swim each day.
It provides the site where dissolved oxygen is lowest, which sets the scale of the graph.

why.correct: Upstream water has not received the farm's nutrients, so it acts as a control: changes below the outfall can be compared with it.
options: Correct: a reference site unaffected by the outfall.
The farm's water enters at distance 0 and flows downstream, so the nutrients do not reach upstream.
The algae drift with the current; the upstream site is not about algae moving.
Upstream oxygen is among the highest dawn readings, not the lowest.

items.q: The farm installs a filter that removes most of the phosphorus from its outflow. Algae in this stream are limited by phosphorus. Predict the dawn oxygen at 3 km the next summer, compared with now.
options: Lower, because less phosphorus means less food for the decomposers in the stream
Higher, because fewer algae grow, so less O₂ is used by respiration and decay
The same, because the farm still releases nitrogen into the stream each day
The same, because dawn oxygen depends on temperature rather than on algae

why.correct: If phosphorus limits the algae, removing it shrinks the bloom. Fewer algae, and less dead algae for decomposers, mean less O₂ used overnight, so dawn O₂ rises toward upstream values.
options: Decomposers feed mainly on dead algae; fewer algae means less decay and less O₂ used, not more.
Correct: cutting the limiting nutrient shrinks the bloom and its oxygen demand.
Extra nitrogen does little when phosphorus is the limiting nutrient.
Temperature was the same at every site, yet dawn O₂ varied with algae, so algae matter.

items.q: How many times higher is the PCB concentration in large fish than in the small fish they eat? Give your answer to one decimal place.

why.correct: 4.5 ÷ 0.9 = 5.0. At each step up this food chain, PCB concentration rises several-fold.

items.q: Which explanation best accounts for the pattern in the table?
options: PCBs are made inside the bodies of predators from chemicals in their prey, so more PCBs form at each higher level.
Larger animals drink more lake water than smaller ones, so they take in more of the PCBs dissolved in the water each day.
PCBs stay in body fat instead of being excreted, and each consumer eats many times its own mass, so they concentrate.
PCBs break down slowly in small organisms but speed up as they move into larger ones, which makes them more concentrated.

why.correct: This is biomagnification. Persistent, fat-soluble PCBs stay in the body; since only about 10% of food becomes new tissue, each predator eats far more prey than its own mass and keeps the PCBs from all of it.
options: PCBs are industrial chemicals; animals do not make them.
The water holds only 0.000004 ppm; drinking cannot explain 4.5 ppm in trout, which take in PCBs mainly in food.
Correct: storage plus the large amount of food eaten.
PCBs break down slowly everywhere; faster breakdown would lower concentrations, not raise them.

items.q: How many times higher is the PCB concentration in gull eggs than in the lake water? Give your answer in millions, to one decimal place (for example, 3.2 for 3.2 million).

why.correct: 90 ÷ 0.000004 = 22,500,000, which is 22.5 million times higher. A toxin barely detectable in water can reach harmful levels at the top of a food web.

items.q: A student claims that because PCB levels in the lake water are tiny, the PCBs pose no risk to wildlife. Which response is best supported by the data?
options: The claim is supported, because 0.000004 ppm is far too low to harm any organism.
The claim is not supported, because gull eggs carry 90 ppm, over 20 million times the water level.
The claim is supported, because PCB levels in phytoplankton are below those in fish.
The claim is not supported, because the water level is higher than in the phytoplankton.

why.correct: Biomagnification turns a tiny concentration in water into a high one in top predators; harm happens where the concentration is high, such as in gull eggs.
options: The water level is low, but animals at the top of the food web are exposed to far more.
Correct: the risk is at the top of the food web.
Low levels in producers fit biomagnification; they do not show the top predators are safe.
The water level (0.000004 ppm) is lower than in phytoplankton (0.02 ppm).

items.q: PCB releases into the lake stop, and PCB levels in the water fall within a few years. Predict which samples will take longest to return to low PCB levels.
options: Phytoplankton, because they are closest to the water and absorb PCBs directly
Zooplankton, because they reproduce faster than the other consumers in the lake
Lake trout and gulls, because they are long-lived and keep stored PCBs in their fat
Lake water, because PCBs dissolve more easily in water than in living tissue

why.correct: Long-lived top predators hold PCBs accumulated over years in their fat and keep eating prey that still carry them, so their levels fall slowly. Short-lived plankton are replaced quickly by new, cleaner individuals.
options: Phytoplankton live days to weeks, so new cells soon reflect the cleaner water.
Fast reproduction replaces zooplankton quickly, so their levels drop sooner.
Correct: long life and fat storage keep PCBs in top predators.
The stem says the water levels fall within a few years; PCBs are fat-soluble, not water-soluble.

items.q: Zebra mussels from Europe reached North America's Great Lakes in ships' ballast water and spread rapidly, while native mussels declined. Which explanation best accounts for their success?
options: Native mussels were already extinct before zebra mussels arrived, leaving the lakes empty of competitors.
They are larger and stronger than the native mussels, so they win most contests for space on the rocky lake bottom.
Ballast water made them more fertile, and the effect lasted for several generations after they arrived.
They left behind the predators and parasites that limit them in Europe, and natives had few ways to resist them.

why.correct: Invasive species often thrive because they leave their natural enemies behind, while native species have not evolved defenses or competitive responses to them.
options: The stem says native mussels declined after the zebra mussels spread, so they were present.
Zebra mussels are small; their success comes from fast reproduction and few enemies, not size.
A trip in ballast water does not change a species' fertility for generations.
Correct: release from natural enemies.

items.q: The CO₂ concentration of the air above an ocean region keeps rising. Predict the effect on each quantity in the surface seawater over the following decades.

variables.name: pH of the seawater
variables.why: More CO₂ dissolves and forms carbonic acid, which releases H⁺, lowering pH.

variables.name: Carbonate ions (CO₃²⁻) available to shell-building animals
variables.why: Extra H⁺ combines with carbonate to form bicarbonate, leaving less carbonate.

variables.name: Rate at which oysters build their shells
variables.why: With less carbonate, building calcium carbonate shells takes more energy and is slower.

variables.name: Number of chromosomes in each oyster's cells
variables.why: Seawater chemistry does not change a species' chromosome number.

why.correct: Ocean acidification: the oceans absorb CO₂, which lowers pH and reduces the carbonate that corals, oysters and some plankton need.

items.q: In a forest, oak caterpillars now hatch about two weeks earlier than 40 years ago because springs are warmer. A songbird that feeds caterpillars to its chicks still lays its eggs at about the same date, timed by day length. Which effect on the songbird is most likely?
options: Chicks get more food, because warmer springs produce more caterpillars for longer.
Chicks hatch earlier too, because warm weather speeds up the incubation of the eggs.
Chicks hatch after the caterpillar peak, so food is short and fewer chicks survive.
Chicks are unaffected, because adult birds can switch to eating seeds in warm years.

why.correct: Warming shifted one event (caterpillar hatching) but not the other (egg laying set by day length), so the peak in chick demand misses the peak in food: a timing mismatch caused by climate change.
options: The caterpillar peak is earlier, not longer; the chicks miss it.
The birds lay at the same date, and incubation length is set by the parent's body heat; the chicks do not catch up two weeks.
Correct: a mismatch between food supply and chick demand.
Nestlings need caterpillars; adults switching food does not feed the chicks.

items.q: A 100 km² forest is cut into twenty separate 1 km² patches with farmland between them, keeping 20 km² of forest. Ten years later, the patches together hold fewer bird species than a single 20 km² block nearby. Which explanation best accounts for this?
options: The farmland adds new bird species, which take over the patches and push most of the forest birds out of them.
Birds in small patches reproduce faster, use up their food sooner and then starve within a few years.
The patches receive less sunlight than a large block, so their trees produce less food for birds.
Small patches hold small populations that are easily lost, and many forest birds avoid the hot, windy edges.

why.correct: Fragmentation makes populations small and isolated, so chance events wipe them out and they are not refilled from nearby; small patches are also mostly edge, unsuitable for deep-forest species.
options: Some farmland birds may enter, but forest birds decline mainly because their patches are too small.
Nothing suggests birds breed faster in small patches; small populations are lost by chance and edge effects.
Small patches get as much sunlight per area; the difference is size, isolation and edge.
Correct: small populations plus edge effects.

items.q: Cod off Newfoundland were fished heavily until the population collapsed and fishing was stopped. Decades later, the population was still far below its earlier size. Which explanation is best supported by population ecology?
options: Cod mature slowly, and the food web changed while they were scarce, so recovery has been slow.
Once a population is heavily fished, its r_max falls to zero and the survivors stop reproducing.
The ban on fishing raised the cod carrying capacity, so the population is now too crowded to grow.
Cod are r-selected, so their numbers stay low for decades after a large fall in population.

why.correct: Cod take several years to reach breeding age, and although each female lays millions of eggs, almost all die young; while they were scarce other species took over their role and some ate young cod, so the population has grown back slowly.
options: Correct: slow maturity plus a changed community.
Fishing removes individuals; the surviving cod can still reproduce.
Ending fishing does not make the population crowded; it is far below its earlier size.
If cod recovered like an r-selected species they would rebound fast; their slow recovery comes from late maturity and the changed food web.

items.q: During an El Niño event, warm surface water off the coast of Peru stops the usual upwelling of cold, nutrient-rich water from the deep. Predict the effect on the coastal food web.
options: Phytoplankton bloom in the warm water, so anchovies and seabirds increase that year.
Phytoplankton decline, so anchovies and the seabirds and sea lions that eat them decline.
The sea lions are the main species affected, because warm water raises their body temperature.
Nothing changes, because the warm water does not reach the bottom of the ocean.

why.correct: Upwelling supplies the nitrogen and phosphorus that limit phytoplankton. Without it, production at the base falls, and the effect passes up the food web: bottom-up control by a natural disturbance.
options: Warm water here means fewer nutrients, so phytoplankton decline rather than bloom.
Correct: less nutrient supply means less food at every level.
Sea lions are endotherms; the main effect on them is through their food supply.
The change is at the surface, where the phytoplankton live, so the food web is affected.

items.q: Select the two human activities that add CO₂ to the atmosphere.
options: Burning natural gas to generate electricity
Clearing and burning a tropical forest for pasture
Planting trees on abandoned farmland
Generating electricity with wind turbines
Restoring a peat bog by blocking its drains

why.correct: Burning fossil fuels and burning or clearing forests both release carbon stored in organic matter as CO₂.
options: Adds CO₂: combustion of a fossil fuel.
Adds CO₂: burning and decay of the forest's carbon, and less photosynthesis afterward.
Removes CO₂: growing trees take in carbon by photosynthesis.
Wind turbines generate electricity without burning fuel.
Waterlogged peat decays slowly, so restoring a bog keeps carbon stored.

items.q: A power plant takes in river water to cool its machinery and returns it 8 °C warmer. Downstream, trout become scarce. Which explanation best accounts for this?
options: Warm water holds more dissolved oxygen, which is toxic to trout at high concentrations in the river.
Warm water holds less dissolved oxygen, and a warmer trout needs more oxygen.
Warm water flows faster than cold water, so trout are unable to swim against the current near the plant.
Warm water kills the algae, so the river has no producers and trout have nothing to eat.

why.correct: This is thermal pollution. Gases dissolve less in warm water, and trout, as ectotherms, have a higher metabolic rate when the water is warmer, so oxygen supply falls just as demand rises.
options: Warm water holds less oxygen, not more.
Correct: less oxygen supply, more oxygen demand.
Temperature does not make water flow faster in this way.
Many algae grow faster in warmer water; the trout's problem is oxygen.

items.q: Put the steps of eutrophication in a coastal sea in order.
options: Heavy rain washes fertilizer from farm fields into rivers.
Nitrate and phosphate reach the sea and algae multiply.
Masses of algae die and sink to deeper water.
Decomposers break down the dead algae, using dissolved oxygen.
Fish leave the area and bottom animals suffocate.

why.correct: Nutrients must arrive before the algae can bloom; the bloom must die before decomposers can use up the oxygen; low oxygen then drives off or kills animals.

items.q: In the 1960s a large lake had frequent algal blooms and low-oxygen bottom water. After phosphate was limited in detergents and sewage treatment improved, phosphorus entering the lake fell by about 60% within ten years, and blooms and low-oxygen areas shrank. Which claim do these data best support?
options: Low oxygen in the bottom water caused the algal blooms, rather than being a result of the blooms.
Detergents killed the algae directly, so removing them had no effect on the blooms.
Phosphorus was limiting algal growth in the lake, and cutting it reduced eutrophication.
Nitrogen, not phosphorus, limited the algae, because blooms continued at a lower level.

why.correct: When the input of a nutrient falls and algal growth falls with it, that nutrient was limiting. Less algae meant less decay and more oxygen in deep water.
options: In eutrophication, blooms come first and low oxygen follows when the algae decay.
Phosphate in detergents fed algae; it did not kill them, and blooms shrank when it was removed.
Correct: reducing the limiting nutrient reversed eutrophication.
Smaller blooms after cutting phosphorus show phosphorus was limiting; leftover blooms do not show nitrogen was.

items.q: Which kind of pollutant is most likely to biomagnify?
options: A water-soluble chemical that the kidneys excrete within a day of exposure
A fat-soluble chemical that is broken down very slowly in the body
A gas that leaves the water quickly and enters the air above a lake
A chemical that decomposers break down within a week in soil

why.correct: To build up from one level to the next, a chemical must stay in the body (fat-soluble) and last (persistent). Mercury, DDT and PCBs fit; quickly excreted or broken-down chemicals do not.
options: Rapid excretion keeps it from building up.
Correct: persistent and fat-soluble.
A gas that leaves the water quickly is not taken in and stored by food webs.
Quick breakdown keeps it from passing up a food chain.

items.q: Which of the following is a natural disturbance rather than a human impact?
options: A volcanic eruption that buries a forest in ash
Runoff of fertilizer into a lake from farm fields
Release of cane toads into a sugar-cane region
Clearing a wetland to build a shopping center

why.correct: A volcanic eruption is a geological event not caused by people.
options: Correct: a natural disturbance.
Fertilizer runoff comes from farming, a human activity.
Releasing a species into a new region is a human action.
Clearing a wetland is habitat loss caused by people.
